opus-5.5.text:
Well, the demos are impressive, and the mechanical engineering progress is real. The hardware has gotten much better and cheaper. But you have to be careful about what a demo actually shows. Many of them are teleoperated, or heavily scripted, or the result of many takes where you only see the one that worked. Even the autonomous ones usually work in a narrow setting the system was trained for.

The real question is: can the robot handle a situation it has never seen? Can a household robot walk into a kitchen it's never been in and clear the table and load the dishwasher? Any ten-year-old can do that the first time. We're not close to that.

The reason is that these systems don't really understand the physical world. Most of the current approaches take the LLM recipe, a big transformer predicting the next action, trained by imitation on lots of demonstrations, and apply it to robotics. That gets you somewhere, but it's not how you get common sense about the physical world. A four-year-old has seen about as much data through vision as the biggest LLMs are trained on in text. And that sensory data is much richer: continuous, high-dimensional, noisy. You can't just predict the next pixel. That doesn't work. Generative models of video waste their capacity predicting details that are fundamentally unpredictable.

What I think is needed are world models, systems that learn abstract representations of the world, mostly from observation, and can predict the consequences of their actions in that abstract space. That's what we've been working on with JEPA, the joint embedding predictive architectures. Once you have a good world model, you can plan: you have an objective, you search for a sequence of actions that achieves it, and you have guardrails. That's how you get zero-shot behavior on new tasks, rather than needing thousands of demonstrations for each one.

So my assessment is: lots of companies are betting that robotics will take off in the next few years, and the hardware will be ready. But the bottleneck is intelligence, not the body. Whether that bet pays off depends on whether we make real progress on world models and planning, not on scaling up imitation learning. I think we will make that progress, but it requires a different paradigm from the one most people are using right now.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation learning would require “thousands of demonstrations for each” task, presenting that as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It explains that a world model predicts action consequences, enabling planning and zero-shot behavior on new tasks without demonstrations for each one.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say you have to be careful about what a demo actually tells you. A demo is a selected success. You see the robot fold the laundry, you don't see the fifty attempts that didn't make it into the video, and you don't see what happens when you move the table six inches or change the lighting. So the first thing is, I don't assess progress from demos. I assess it from what the system can do reliably, in conditions it was not specifically trained for, and demos are basically designed to hide that information.

Now, is there real progress? Yes, absolutely. The hardware has gotten better, the control is smoother, and the idea of training on large amounts of teleoperation data and video has clearly moved things forward compared to five years ago. I'm not dismissive of that. But there's a big difference between an impressive demo and a system that has a model of the physical world.

And that's the thing I keep coming back to. The current approach, for the most part, is to take the recipe that worked for language, which is autoregressive prediction of tokens, and apply it to actions. And language is a very particular case. It's discrete, it's low-bandwidth, it's already a compressed representation of the world that humans produced. The physical world is not like that. It's continuous, high-dimensional, mostly unpredictable at the pixel level, and you cannot just predict every detail of what happens next. If you try, the system wastes all its capacity on things that don't matter, like the exact texture of the carpet, instead of learning the stuff that does matter, like whether the object will fall if you let go.

So what I think is missing, and what the demos don't show, is a world model. A representation that lets the robot predict the consequences of its actions at an abstract level, so it can plan. A ten-year-old can clear the dinner table the first time they're asked, without ten thousand demonstrations. A cat can plan a sequence of jumps onto a counter it has never been on. We don't have that. Nothing close. And that's not a scale problem, it's an architecture problem. You're not going to get there by collecting more teleop data and training a bigger transformer.

This is why I've been pushing on things like JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, where you learn to predict in representation space rather than in input space. You learn what's predictable and you ignore what's not. That's the kind of thing I think will eventually give robots common sense, in the sense of an intuitive understanding of physics and objects and causality. And then you can do planning on top of it, with actual objectives and guardrails, instead of just hoping the policy generalizes.

So the honest answer is, the demos are real engineering progress, and they are also marketing. The companies have strong incentives to show you the one in ten that worked. And I'd say the Moravec paradox is still very much alive. We have systems that pass the bar exam and we still don't have a robot that can reliably load a dishwasher in a kitchen it hasn't seen. When that changes, it won't be because of a bigger LLM. It'll be because somebody figured out how to make machines learn how the world works by watching it, the way babies and animals do. And we're not there yet, despite the videos.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes reliance on more teleoperation data and mentions 10,000 demonstrations, but does not identify imitation learning’s need for large amounts of demonstrations for each new robotic task.

r002.rationale: It says a world model predicts action consequences at an abstract level so a robot can plan, and illustrates handling tasks or environments it has not encountered before.

astra-6.text:
The demos are impressive, but the question is how much generality is behind them. You can get a robot to perform a particular task very well with enough engineering and training data. What happens when you change the object, the room, or the task? Can it adapt without collecting thousands of new demonstrations?

Robotics makes a fundamental limitation very clear: a system needs to understand the consequences of its actions. It needs some model of the world that allows it to predict, plan, and correct its mistakes. Producing a plausible sequence of actions is useful, but it doesn’t by itself establish that capability.

So I’m encouraged by the progress. But I would look less at the most spectacular successful trial and more at how reliably the system handles situations it hasn’t encountered before. That’s where you find out how much progress you’ve actually made.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot may need thousands of new demonstrations to adapt when the task or setting changes, identifying task-specific demonstration data as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says a world model can predict, plan, and correct mistakes, and separately raises performance in unfamiliar situations. It does not clearly state that those predictions enable solving new tasks without training on them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress is impressive, but a demonstration is not the same thing as a robust system. The question is: how much training went into that particular task, and what happens when you change the conditions? Can the robot handle an object it hasn’t seen, recover when something goes wrong, or figure out a new task without collecting thousands of additional demonstrations?

Robotics forces us to confront something that language alone doesn’t solve: understanding the physical world well enough to predict the consequences of actions. A robot needs some kind of world model. It needs to anticipate what will happen, consider different actions, and plan toward a goal.

So I’m encouraged by the demos. But I would judge progress by how much those systems generalize, how efficiently they learn, and how reliably they work outside the circumstances of the demonstration. That’s where the really difficult problems are.

r001.rationale: The response describes needing thousands of additional demonstrations to learn a new task and frames that as a challenge for robotics systems.

r002.rationale: It says a world model lets a robot anticipate action outcomes and plan toward a goal, while asking whether it can handle a new task without collecting additional demonstrations.
